studies that firmly established ADR as a predictor of patient outcomes. In a large screening cohort, one study found that patients whose colonoscopies were performed by endoscopists with ADRs <20% faced a 10- to 12-fold higher risk of interval CRC compared to those with ADRs ≥20% [ ]. Similarly, another large retrospective study demonstrated that each 1% increase in ADR was associated with a 3% reduction in the risk of interval CRC, advanced-stage CRC, and cancer-related mortality [ ]. These findings led prominent societies such as the U.S. Multi-Society Task Force on Colorectal Cancer to establish minimum ADR benchmarks of 25% overall, with sex-specific thresholds of 30% for men and 20% for women [ ]. Beyond its prognostic significance, ADR also reflects important epidemiologic trends. As adenoma prevalence has increased, the American Society for Gastrointestinal Endoscopy (ASGE) now recommends measuring ADR in patients aged ≥45 years and suggests a minimum performance target of 35%, with sex-specific thresholds of 40% for men and 30% for women [ ]. This is based on accumulating data showing that ADRs have risen steadily over the past decade, with a mean of 38% in U.S. practices by 2018, and that the risk of PCCRC (post-colonoscopy colorectal cancer) continues to decrease with ADRs above 35–40% [ ]. A recent large-scale retrospective study of nearly 19,000 average-risk individuals in rural China revealed that ADR increases significantly after the age of 45, especially in men, lending support to the revised CRC screening guidelines that recommend initiating screening at age 45 [ ]. However, while ADR is a reliable measure of detection, it does not capture all dimensions of endoscopic performance. One major limitation of ADR is its binary structure: it registers whether at least one adenoma is found but provides no information about the total number of adenomas, their location, or whether they were completely resected. As a result, it is vulnerable to the “one and done” phenomenon, in which an endoscopist may reduce inspection intensity after identifying a single lesion [ ]. It also fails to measure adenoma removal quality, which is equally critical for CRC prevention. Furthermore, ADR can be influenced by external factors such as patient demographics, referral population, and even interobserver variability in histopathologic diagnosis [ ]. To address these shortcomings, complementary metrics have been proposed. One such measure, Adenoma Under the Curve (AUC), incorporates both the rate of adenoma detection and the number of adenomas per colonoscopy. In one comparative study, AUC revealed a 25% performance gap between academic and community settings, despite only a 10% difference in ADR, suggesting it may better capture the depth of mucosal inspection [ ]. Additional metrics such as advanced ADR (focused on high-risk adenomas) and adenoma per colonoscopy (APC) are under investigation, though none have yet surpassed ADR as the core benchmark. Technological advances such as Endocuff-assisted colonoscopy and linked color imaging (LCI) have been shown to significantly improve ADR across a range of practice settings [ ]. Among these, AI-assisted systems appear particularly promising for standardizing detection performance and reducing inter-operator variability. As colonoscopy continues to evolve with the integration of real-time computer-aided detection and enhanced imaging tools, ADR remains a foundational metric. 3. Serrated Lesion Detection (SPDR) While conventional adenomas have long been the primary focus of colonoscopy quality improvement efforts, there is growing recognition that serrated lesions, particularly sessile serrated lesions and traditional serrated adenomas (TSAs), contribute significantly to colorectal cancer burden, especially in the proximal colon [ ]. Serrated polyps are now understood to be responsible for up to 20–30% of sporadic CRCs [ ]. Unlike adenomas, serrated lesions often exhibit a flat morphology, indistinct borders, and a mucus cap, making them easy to miss during routine inspection. To address this diagnostic blind spot, the serrated polyp detection rate (SPDR) has emerged as an important, though still evolving, quality metric. SPDR is typically defined as the proportion of colonoscopies in which at least one serrated lesion (usually an SSL or TSA) is identified. Although benchmark thresholds have not been as well established compared to those for ADR, recent literature suggests target SPDR values ranging from 5 to 10% may reflect adequate detection skill [ ]. The establishment of universal SPDR benchmarks is inherently challenging due to substantial heterogeneity in serrated lesion prevalence across patient populations, procedural indications, and colonic segments, which limits the generalizability of fixed threshold targets. Variability in SPDR has been observed across endoscopists, sometimes exceeding the variability seen with ADR, raising concern that serrated lesions are being inconsistently detected and under-reported [ ]. This inconsistency is particularly problematic given that SSLs account for 20–30% of sporadic colorectal cancers and disproportionately contribute to interval cancers due to their flat morphology and subtle endoscopic features. Despite its promise, several limitations hinder widespread SPDR adoption. A key challenge in implementing SPDR as

inherently challenging due to substantial heterogeneity in serrated lesion prevalence across patient populations, procedural indications, and colonic segments, which limits the generalizability of fixed threshold targets. Variability in SPDR has been observed across endoscopists, sometimes exceeding the variability seen with ADR, raising concern that serrated lesions are being inconsistently detected and under-reported [ ]. This inconsistency is particularly problematic given that SSLs account for 20–30% of sporadic colorectal cancers and disproportionately contribute to interval cancers due to their flat morphology and subtle endoscopic features. Despite its promise, several limitations hinder widespread SPDR adoption. A key challenge in implementing SPDR as a standard quality metric lies in the interobserver variability of serrated lesion diagnosis by pathologists, as well as limited awareness and training among endoscopists to recognize subtle endoscopic features. Moreover, studies have shown that SPDR is not strongly correlated with ADR, reinforcing the need for a separate, dedicated focus on serrated lesion detection during colonoscopy [ ]. Population-level factors such as referral bias, case mix, and demographic differences may further influence SPDR, contributing to wide performance dispersion and complicating direct comparisons between endoscopists and practice settings [ ]. Still, serrated lesion detection is clinically critical, as patients with SSLs, particularly proximal or ≥10 mm lesions, face a higher risk of future advanced neoplasia [ ]. Improvements in SPDR, therefore, have the potential to significantly enhance colonoscopy’s preventive effectiveness. Emerging strategies, including prolonged right colon withdrawal, retroflexion, enhanced imaging modalities such as NBI, TXI, or Linked Color Imaging, and AI-assisted detection systems, have shown promise in improving serrated lesion recognition, although their implementation remains inconsistent and requires further guideline standardization [ , , ]. To overcome benchmark variability, large registry-based datasets may enable risk-adjusted or percentile-based SPDR modeling that accounts for patient demographics, indication, bowel preparation quality, and procedural factors. Looking ahead, future directions include the development of composite quality models integrating ADR, SPDR, and adenomas per colonoscopy into weighted indices that better reflect both major colorectal carcinogenesis pathways [ ]. Large-scale registries such as GIQuIC will be crucial for validating SPDR benchmarks, supporting longitudinal evaluation of interventions, and standardizing data collection to reduce variability in lesion classification [ ]. These efforts will be essential before SPDR can be routinely adopted as a national quality indicator alongside ADR. 4. Cecal Intubation Rate (CIR) Complete visualization of the colon is fundamental to the effectiveness of colonoscopy as a screening and diagnostic tool. The cecal intubation rate (CIR) measures the proportion of colonoscopies in which the endoscopist successfully advances the colonoscope to the cecum, typically confirmed by identifying the appendiceal orifice and ileocecal valve, as shown in . The CIR is one of the consistently validated quality indicators because incomplete examinations correlate with missed proximal neoplasia, higher rates of interval colorectal cancer, and the need for early repeat procedures [ ]. High CIR reflects adequate technique in navigating tortuous or angulated anatomy and the ability to maintain a luminal view through suctioning, insufflation, and position changes. Studies have shown that incomplete colonoscopies are significantly associated with an increased risk of proximal interval CRC, which highlights the importance of achieving complete examination when possible [ ]. After the recognition of CIR as an important colonoscopy quality indicator, clear benchmarks were established. For screening and surveillance colonoscopies, the recommended minimum CIR is ≥95% [ ]. Lower thresholds may be allowed for purely diagnostic procedures where patient factors such as obstructing tumors or severe colitis limit advancement. However, these cases should be carefully documented to distinguish technical limitations from operator performance. Persistent CIR values below benchmark levels require review of case logs, technical training, or evaluation of outside contributors, such as bowel preparation quality. Despite its strengths, the CIR is not a comprehensive measure of colonoscopy quality. A technically complete examination does not guarantee adequate mucosal inspection, particularly if the endoscopist advances rapidly, fails to control looping, or does not optimize visualization during insertion. The CIR can also be influenced by factors outside of operator control, such as bowel preparation, patient discomfort thresholds, and institutional support for adequate sedation. Nonetheless, as colonoscopy technology and adjunctive tools have improved, CIR has become a valuable metric, with contemporary practices consistently achieving rates above 95% [ ]. 5. Polyp Detection Rate Polyp detection rate (PDR) is defined as the proportion of colonoscopies in which at least one polyp of any histologic type is identified [ ]. Although less specific than adenoma detection rate (ADR), PDR remains a widely used metric in complement to ADR because it does not require pathology correlation and is a quick estimate of mucosal inspection quality. PDR also covers a broader range of detected lesions, including hyperplastic polyps, inflammatory polyps, and serrated lesions, all of which may be clinically relevant depending on location and size. Detection Rate Polyp detection rate (PDR) is defined as the proportion of colonoscopies in which at least one polyp of any histologic type is identified [ ]. Although less specific than adenoma detection rate (ADR), PDR remains a widely used metric in complement to ADR because it does not require pathology correlation and is a quick estimate of mucosal inspection quality. PDR also covers a broader range of detected lesions, including hyperplastic polyps, inflammatory polyps, and serrated lesions, all of which may be clinically relevant depending on location and size. The primary value of PDR is its practicality. Metrics that require pathology, such as ADR, require accurate integration of histologic data, which is not reliably feasible across all practice settings. PDR relies solely on endoscopic documentation and enables immediate monitoring and comparison of detection performance [ ]. Multiple studies show a strong correlation between PDR and ADR, making PDR a reasonable substitute for ADR in settings where pathology data are incomplete [ ]. This correlation allows institutions to flag potential underperformance earlier while awaiting confirmed histologic metrics. Despite its utility, PDR has significant limitations. Because it includes all polyp types, it is vulnerable to inflation through the removal or documentation of clinically insignificant lesions. This weakness makes it less reliable as a true cancer-prevention indicator. Additionally, PDR does not distinguish between adenomatous and serrated lesions and does not account for the total number of lesions found during an examination [ ]. As a result, PDR does not meaningfully reflect the thoroughness of mucosal inspection or lesion recognition complexity. The metric also tends to be less stable across varying patient populations because polyp prevalence is influenced more strongly by demographic factors than adenoma prevalence. Benchmark values for PDR vary across studies and institutions, but many programs consider 40% an expected minimum in average-risk screening populations, with higher targets in practices that have fully adopted high-definition imaging [ ]. Nonetheless, PDR should not be interpreted in isolation. It functions best as an adjunctive measure that supports broader quality monitoring, identifies trends in detection behavior, and provides rapid-feedback signals when histology-linked metrics are unavailable. When interpreted alongside other metrics, PDR helps create a more comprehensive picture of endoscopic detection performance while avoiding excessive reliance on a single indicator. 6. Adenomas per Positive Colonoscopy Adenomas per positive colonoscopy (APPC) represents the average number of adenomas identified among colonoscopies in which at least one adenoma is found. Unlike adenoma detection rate (ADR), which only captures whether the endoscopist identified any adenoma, APPC provides a quantitative assessment of mucosal inspection depth while avoiding the extreme variability seen with metrics that average adenoma counts across all procedures, including negative exams [ ]. By focusing solely on examinations where at least one adenoma was detected, APPC reduces statistical interference and offers a more stable estimate of true detection performance. The strength of APPC is its ability to describe differences in lesion-finding behavior that ADR alone conceals. Two endoscopists may have identical ADRs yet differ substantially in how thoroughly they evaluate the colon once the first adenoma is found. Studies have shown that APPC correlates more strongly than ADR with metrics tied to overall detection burden, such as adenomas per colonoscopy [ ]. APPC may more effectively reveal underperformance in experienced endoscopists for whom ADR meets minimum thresholds but whose inspection technique remains suboptimal [ ]. Nonetheless, APPC is not without its limitations. Because it excludes negative colonoscopies entirely, it artificially narrows the dataset and may overrepresent endoscopists who work with higher-risk populations. This selective averaging can obscure meaningful differences in patient mix and does not reflect the full procedural portfolio of the operator. APPC also shares the vulnerabilities of other count-based metrics in that it can be influenced by over-removal of clinically insignificant diminutive lesions and is sensitive to pathology interpretation consistency. Additionally, benchmarks for APPC remain undefined, with no consensus existing on threshold targets, limiting its use as a stand-alone metric. 7. Advanced Adenoma Detection Rate The advanced adenoma detection rate (AADR) measures the proportion of colonoscopies in which at least one advanced adenoma is detected. Advanced adenomas are typically defined as adenomas ≥10 mm, those with villous or tubulovillous histology, or those demonstrating high-grade dysplasia [ ]. Because these lesions represent the subset of precancerous polyps with the highest malignant potential, AADR is an assessment of an endoscopist’s ability to detect pathology that most directly influences colorectal cancer prevention. The AADR’s strength is its clinical significance. Multiple studies have shown that the presence of advanced adenomas strongly predicts future advanced neoplasia and colorectal cancer, making their detection a critical objective of screening colonoscopy [ ]. By isolating clinically consequential lesions, AADR complements broader detection metrics like ADR. AADR provides a more outcome-driven approach, emphasizing detection of the lesions most important to long-term patient risk stratification [

]. Because these lesions represent the subset of precancerous polyps with the highest malignant potential, AADR is an assessment of an endoscopist’s ability to detect pathology that most directly influences colorectal cancer prevention. The AADR’s strength is its clinical significance. Multiple studies have shown that the presence of advanced adenomas strongly predicts future advanced neoplasia and colorectal cancer, making their detection a critical objective of screening colonoscopy [ ]. By isolating clinically consequential lesions, AADR complements broader detection metrics like ADR. AADR provides a more outcome-driven approach, emphasizing detection of the lesions most important to long-term patient risk stratification [ ]. Despite its conceptual value, AADR is limited by substantial statistical and practical constraints. Advanced adenomas are relatively uncommon, which leads to significant variability in measured rates, especially for low-volume endoscopists. As a result, AADR is more sensitive to random variation than ADR, and year-over-year comparisons often lack stability [ ]. Additionally, AADR is heavily influenced by patient demographics, referral patterns, and underlying population risk. Endoscopists serving older or higher-risk patient populations may appear to have superior AADR, independent of technique, whereas others practicing in younger or lower-risk settings may struggle to meet expected ranges despite adequate performance. 8. Withdrawal Time Withdrawal time is one of the most validated surrogate markers of colonoscopy quality, with numerous studies demonstrating a strong, positive correlation between longer withdrawal times and higher adenoma detection rates. For example, a landmark analysis found that each additional minute of withdrawal time was associated with a 3.6% increase in ADR [ ]. Reflecting on this evidence, leading professional societies recommend a minimum withdrawal time of 6 min (excluding time spent on interventions like polyp removal) to ensure comprehensive mucosal inspection [ ]. Adherence to this 6 min standard is associated with a reduction in the incidence of interval colorectal cancer, underscoring its importance for preventive effectiveness [ ]. Notably, studies have shown that extending withdrawal time beyond 6 min, particularly up to 9 min, can yield even greater improvements in ADR, especially in the proximal colon and among less experienced endoscopists [ ]. Although a 6 min withdrawal serves as a widely acknowledged baseline, it may need to be exceeded in higher-risk scenarios, such as patients with a history of adenomas or suboptimal bowel preparation, to maximize detection and preventive impact. 9. Current Barriers to Quality Colonoscopies Despite standardized guidelines for colonoscopy performance, inter-endoscopist variability remains a major barrier to consistent quality. To that end, prior studies have demonstrated that ADR can significantly differ between practitioners even within the same institution. This variation reflects differences in not only expertise, such as withdrawal technique and thoroughness with mucosal inspection, but also personal preference, like utilization of adjunctive technologies. The basis of such variability is multifactorial; differences may stem from training background and procedural volume, with higher-volume endoscopists often achieving higher ADR yield [ , ]. Institutional culture can also play a role, as centers with robust quality monitoring programs often display less inter-practitioner variability compared to those lacking structured feedback systems. Furthermore, even when lesions are resected, discrepancies in pathology interpretation can undermine quality. For instance, a histologic distinction between hyperplastic polyps and SSLs is often subtle, and inter-pathologist agreement is imperfect [ ]. Other barriers to colonoscopy quality arise from factors that extend beyond the endoscopist’s direct technical skill. Time pressure and scheduling demands can influence behavior in subtle but important ways. High procedural volumes and productivity pressures have been associated with shortened withdrawal times and less meticulous mucosal inspection, which are both linked to lower adenoma detection rates [ , ]. Inadequate bowel preparation remains one of the most significant obstacles to effective screening. Poor preparation reduces mucosal visibility, particularly in the right colon, where flat lesions and retained debris are more common. This is consistently associated with higher miss rates for advanced neoplasia [ ]. Preparation quality is highly variable and may be impacted by patient-related factors such as adherence, comorbidities (e.g., constipation, diabetes, or opioid use), and the type of regimen prescribed [ ]. Suboptimal preps often necessitate repeat colonoscopies, which drive up costs, increase patient inconvenience, and undermine screening effectiveness. In conjunction with poor bowel preparation, patient-specific factors and anatomical variability inherently introduce additional challenges. Prior abdominal surgeries, particularly gastrectomies and hysterectomies, were associated with a lower cecal intubation rate and incomplete procedures [ ]. Additionally, several studies have also suggested a potential U-shaped relationship between central adiposity, as represented by body mass index (BMI), and relative procedural difficulty. Specifically, both high and low BMIs are positively correlated with colonoscopy times and incompleteness [ ]. Fatigue and human factors also play a meaningful role. Endoscopist fatigue, whether from extended procedure lists, overnight call duties, or cognitive overload, has been associated with impaired performance, including lower ADRs, poorer withdrawal quality, and even higher complication rates

Additionally, several studies have also suggested a potential U-shaped relationship between central adiposity, as represented by body mass index (BMI), and relative procedural difficulty. Specifically, both high and low BMIs are positively correlated with colonoscopy times and incompleteness [ ]. Fatigue and human factors also play a meaningful role. Endoscopist fatigue, whether from extended procedure lists, overnight call duties, or cognitive overload, has been associated with impaired performance, including lower ADRs, poorer withdrawal quality, and even higher complication rates [ ]. These findings emphasize that quality is not solely a matter of training or vigilance, but also of managing systemic pressures and human limitations. Addressing these barriers requires both institutional support and ongoing monitoring of quality metrics. 10. Strategies to Improve Quality Parameters Standardized training programs, integrating both didactic instruction and hands-on practical experience, play a vital role in reducing inter-endoscopist variability and reinforcing consistent colonoscopy techniques. For example, an endoscopic quality improvement initiative demonstrated that structured training combined with personalized feedback led to an absolute increase of approximately 11% in ADR across practitioners [ ]. Such programs are particularly important for improving the detection of subtle lesions like sessile serrated lesions and flat adenomas, which are frequently associated with interval cancers. By emphasizing lesion recognition and lesion resection quality, these interventions help close gaps in preventive performance. Furthermore, routine auditing and continuous feedback against quality metrics, such as ADR and withdrawal time, enable endoscopists to compare their performance against institutional standards and national benchmarks [ ]. While detection-based metrics such as ADR and SPDR are central to colonoscopy quality assessment, they represent only one component of effective colorectal cancer prevention. Complete and durable resection of identified lesions is equally critical, as incomplete polyp removal has been implicated as a major contributor to interval colorectal cancer [ , ]. Prior studies have demonstrated that residual or recurrent neoplasia at polypectomy sites, particularly following removal of large or sessile lesions, accounts for a substantial proportion of post-colonoscopy cancers. As a result, quality indicators related to resection technique, margin assessment, and surveillance adherence are increasingly recognized as complementary measures of procedural effectiveness [ , , ]. In addition, post-polypectomy outcomes, including adverse events, recurrence rates, and long-term associations with interval colorectal cancer, provide important downstream validation of colonoscopy quality [ ]. Although these outcome-based metrics are more challenging to standardize and require longitudinal follow-up, they represent clinically meaningful endpoints that link procedural performance to patient-centered outcomes. Integrating detection metrics with measures of resection quality and long-term outcomes may therefore offer a more comprehensive framework for assessing colonoscopy quality. The right colon is a frequent site for missed lesions, largely due to its complex anatomy and higher prevalence of flat serrated lesions. Retroflexion following cecal intubation provides an alternate viewing angle, uncovering lesions hidden behind folds or flexures. In a multicenter randomized trial, a second examination of the right colon, whether by retroflexion or a second forward view, improved ADR by approximately 11%, without significant procedural complications and with minimal additional time (about 1.6 min) [ ]. Similarly, a 2022 study reported that this maneuver increased right-sided ADR by 5.5% [ ]. Despite the potential benefits, the practice of retroflexion is not universally adopted, likely due to concerns over mucosal trauma and increased procedure time. However, data show a high success rate in performing retroflexion (up to 91.9%) and an exceptionally low adverse event rate of just 0.03% [ ]. Thus, with proper training, retroflexion is both safe and time-efficient, and can be a valuable adjunct, especially in high-risk patients. Other challenging segments, such as the hepatic flexure and sigmoid colon, may also benefit from second-look strategies, which can be conducted immediately following cecal intubation or the withdrawal phase. Though adopting second-look strategies slightly increases procedural times, such strategies have consistently shown measurable improvements in ADR and hold promise for reducing interval colorectal cancers [ ]. 11. Enhanced Imaging and Technical Modifications Several technical innovations have been developed to overcome the limitations of standard colonoscopy and to improve lesion detection. Distal attachment devices have been developed to improve mucosal visualization by mechanically altering the field of view during colonoscopy. The most established of these is transparent cap-assisted colonoscopy (CAC), in which a clear cap is affixed to the distal end of the colonoscope. The cap maintains a uniform distance between the scope and mucosa, flattens folds, and prevents mucosal collapse into the lens. Randomized trials and meta-analyses demonstrate that CAC not only facilitates cecal intubation by preventing mucosal collapse into the lens but also modestly increases ADR and reduces intubation times [ , ]. Building on this principle, Endocuff-assisted colonoscopy (EAC) employs a disposable cap with flexible projections that fold back during

altering the field of view during colonoscopy. The most established of these is transparent cap-assisted colonoscopy (CAC), in which a clear cap is affixed to the distal end of the colonoscope. The cap maintains a uniform distance between the scope and mucosa, flattens folds, and prevents mucosal collapse into the lens. Randomized trials and meta-analyses demonstrate that CAC not only facilitates cecal intubation by preventing mucosal collapse into the lens but also modestly increases ADR and reduces intubation times [ , ]. Building on this principle, Endocuff-assisted colonoscopy (EAC) employs a disposable cap with flexible projections that fold back during insertion and splay outward on withdrawal. Endoscopic attachments, such as the Endocuff Vision and transparent caps, are simple mechanical devices designed to optimize mucosal visualization. Both function by flattening folds and stabilizing the distal tip of the scope, thereby exposing mucosa that might otherwise remain hidden. Randomized controlled trials have demonstrated that Endocuff-assisted colonoscopy improves ADR, particularly in the proximal colon, where folds and flexures are more prevalent [ , ]. These devices are especially valuable in patients with challenging anatomy, including those with a tortuous or redundant colon, representing a refinement of earlier transparent cap technology. Collectively, distal attachment devices highlight how simple mechanical innovations can enhance inspection thoroughness and reduce the risk of missed lesions. Water-aided techniques represent another approach, where water is used instead of air to distend the lumen and improve mucosal visibility. This is done by washing debris and minimizing bubbles. In particular, the water-exchange method permits cleansing and inspection simultaneously during insertion. It has been shown to improve ADR, reduce patient discomfort, and lower sedation requirements, albeit with slightly longer insertion times [ , ]. Chromoendoscopy is another valuable asset for lesion recognition, especially in patients at increased risk. It encompasses both dye-spray and virtual modalities and is a widely studied adjunct aimed at improving detection beyond standard white-light endoscopy. Dye-based methods enhance mucosal contrast and have been shown to improve neoplasia detection compared with white-light endoscopy [ ]. Beyond traditional dye-spray, virtual chromoendoscopy technologies, such as linked color imaging (LCI) and narrow band imaging (NBI), leverage altered light spectra and digital post-processing to highlight subtle lesions. Recent evidence indicates that these tools enhance the detection of SSLs and aid in delineating lesion margins prior to resection [ ]. Together, these techniques underscore how adjunctive technologies can augment mucosal visualization, facilitate thorough inspection, and ultimately improve the preventive effectiveness of colonoscopy. 12. Role of Artificial Intelligence in Colonoscopy Quality Metrics Advancements in endoscopic technology are continually introducing innovative modalities designed to minimize limitations in colonoscopy performance and maximize patient outcomes. Computer-aided detection (CADe) systems integrate artificial intelligence into colonoscopy workflows to assist with real-time polyp identification. Several studies have shown that CADe can significantly improve ADR across varying levels of endoscopist experience, helping buffer inter-operator variability [ , ]. While CADe offers consistency and reduces fatigue-related performance declines, its heightened sensitivity often results in false positives due to stool or bubbles, and necessitates investment in compatible imaging systems and workflow integration [ ]. Alongside CADe is computer-aided diagnosis (CADx), an AI-powered model designed to systematically differentiate between adenomatous and non-adenomatous diminutive polyps in real time. CADx may be leveraged as an optical biopsy to guide resection decisions. Prior research has revealed that in approximately 90% of patient cases, CADx-informed polypectomies were confirmed to be in accordance with histology guidelines. CADx would further contribute to maximizing endoscopist objectivity, as well as reducing the burden of unnecessary polypectomies for patients [ ]. Another application of AI lies in the assessment of bowel preparation, as suboptimal preparation significantly reduces ADR yield. After being trained with the Boston Bowel Preparation Scale (BBPS), AI systems have demonstrated success in evaluating preparation thoroughness and recommending re-cleansing as needed, ultimately manifesting in a reduced adenoma miss rate (AMR) [ ]. Furthermore, real-time quality tracking systems such as the Automatic Quality Control System (AQCS) represent an emerging frontier. AQCS has been demonstrated in a randomized controlled trial to increase ADR, enhance withdrawal technique, and improve bowel preparation metrics through intra-procedural feedback [ , ]. Collectively, these innovations demonstrate how AI is destined to transform colonoscopy into a more standardized, data-driven, and optimized procedure. Despite these demonstrated benefits, the widespread adoption of AI-assisted detection and advanced imaging technologies remains constrained by cost, infrastructure requirements, and workflow integration challenges, particularly in community-based practices. Although AI-assisted and technology-enhanced colonoscopy may improve detection, limitations related to false positives, workflow integration, training demands, and cost-effectiveness, particularly in community and lower-resource settings, should be considered when evaluating broader adoption. Upfront capital investment, software licensing, hardware compatibility, and the need for endoscopist and staff training may limit accessibility outside of high-resource or academic centers, raising concerns about uneven adoption across practice settings [ , ]. Although AI-assisted and technology-enhanced colonoscopy may improve detection, limitations related to false positives, workflow integration, training demands, and cost-effectiveness, particularly in community and lower-resource settings, should be considered when evaluating broader adoption. Upfront capital investment, software licensing, hardware compatibility, and the need for endoscopist and staff training may limit accessibility outside of high-resource or academic centers, raising concerns about uneven adoption across practice settings [ , ]. Integration into existing workflows may also introduce challenges related to alert fatigue, procedure efficiency, and interoperability with endoscopy reporting systems [ , ]. Addressing these barriers through scalable platforms, registry-supported implementation studies, and cost-effectiveness analyses will be essential to ensure that technological advances in colonoscopy quality do not inadvertently widen disparities in colorectal cancer prevention. 13. Generalizability Across Practice Settings While much of the evidence supporting colonoscopy quality metrics and advanced detection technologies is derived from large academic centers, national registries, and high-resource healthcare systems, the translation of these approaches to community-based and lower-resource practice settings requires careful consideration. Community practices perform the majority of screening colonoscopies worldwide and may face constraints related to procedure time, staffing, access to advanced imaging platforms, and artificial intelligence tools. In these settings, foundational quality measures such as adequate bowel preparation, complete examination to the cecum, sufficient withdrawal time, and adherence to surveillance guidelines remain critical in preventive effectiveness. Lastly, scalable quality improvement strategies may offer practical pathways to improving colonoscopy quality across diverse healthcare environments. 14. Conclusions Colonoscopy remains the cornerstone of colorectal cancer prevention, but its effectiveness is directly tied to the quality of mucosal inspection and lesion detection. The ADR has long served as the most validated quality benchmark, strongly linked to interval cancer risk and widely adopted in practice. However, ADR alone is insufficient to capture the full spectrum of colorectal neoplasia. The growing recognition of the serrated pathway, which accounts for up to a third of sporadic CRCs, has led to the emergence of the SPDR as a complementary metric. Despite its promise, SPDR faces barriers including interobserver variability, inconsistent benchmarks, and variable adoption across practices. Looking forward, colonoscopy quality assessment will likely need to evolve from reliance on single metrics toward multidimensional frameworks that better reflect inspection thoroughness, lesion burden, and procedural completeness. Composite approaches incorporating ADR, SPDR, adenomas per colonoscopy, and withdrawal time may provide a more nuanced and clinically meaningful evaluation of endoscopist performance. Despite their utility, colonoscopy quality metrics remain the subject of ongoing debate. Concerns include the potential for metric-driven behavior, increasing administrative burden associated with monitoring multiple indicators, and uncertainty regarding whether incremental improvements in detection metrics consistently translate into meaningful patient-centered outcomes. Large-scale registries and standardized pathology reporting will be essential to validating these models and establishing generalizable benchmarks across diverse practice settings. Conceptually, colonoscopy quality metrics may be best understood within a tiered framework. Foundational measures such as cecal intubation rate, adequate bowel preparation, and withdrawal time ensure procedural completeness. Detection-based metrics such as ADR and SPDR assess inspection quality across both adenomatous and serrated pathways. Finally, outcome-linked measures, including adenomas per colonoscopy and interval colorectal cancer rates, provide downstream validation of clinical effectiveness. Within this model, ADR remains a necessary baseline benchmark, while complementary metrics may be selectively emphasized based on patient population, practice setting, and available resources. Importantly, colonoscopy quality assessment should also account for patient-centered outcomes, including procedural burden, complication risk, anxiety related to surveillance intensity, and the role of shared decision-making. Aligning quality indicators with value-based care principles will be essential to ensuring that quality improvement efforts translate into meaningful benefits for patients. Technological innovations, including image-enhanced endoscopy, distal attachment devices, and artificial intelligence-assisted detection, are poised to further reduce inter-operator variability and improve detection of subtle lesions. As these tools become increasingly integrated into routine practice, quality metrics must evolve in parallel to ensure that performance assessment remains outcome-driven and clinically relevant. Ultimately, refining colonoscopy quality evaluation through evidence-based, integrated frameworks has the potential to enhance consistency, equity, and preventive effectiveness in colorectal cancer screening.

chunks.content: Introduction Pancreatic leaks and fistulas are severe complications of acute and chronic pancreatitis and of pancreatic surgery or trauma. Pancreatic leaks and fistulas increase the risk of intra-abdominal infection, systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS), multiple-organ failure, and, in severe cases, death [ – ]. Endoscopic retrograde pancreatic duct drainage (ERPD) is a minimally invasive option with demonstrated efficacy [ ]. It reduces the transpapillary pressure gradient, restores ductal continuity, and facilitates drainage of pancreatic juice through the papilla, thereby promoting fistula closure [ ]. Although several studies have evaluated outcomes of ERPD for pancreatic leaks and fistulas, most were limited by small sample sizes and single-center designs. Reported clinical success rates vary widely, ranging from 55% to 75%, due to different definitions of clinical success across studies [ , ]. Studies on the effectiveness and safety of endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) for managing pancreatic leaks and fistulas remain controversial [ , ]. This multicenter retrospective study aimed to assess the technical and clinical success of ERPD in patients with pancreatic leaks and fistulas, to analyze the association between fistula classification, drainage method, and therapeutic outcomes, and to identify predictors of treatment success. Materials and methods Study design and patient selection A retrospective analysis was conducted of 106 consecutive patients with pancreatic fistula caused by pancreatitis, surgical procedures, or trauma, who were treated between July 2007 and August 2023 at the First and Seventh Medical Centers of the Chinese PLA General Hospital, the Second Hospital of Hebei Medical University, and Henan Provincial People’s Hospital. This study was conducted in strict accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. The study protocol was approved by the Institutional Review Board of the Ethics Committee of the Chinese PLA General Hospital (Approval No. S2024-645-01) and by the respective institutional review boards of all participating centers. The requirement for individual informed consent was waived by the Ethics Committee of the Chinese PLA General Hospital because this study was a retrospective analysis of anonymized medical records and involved no intervention outside routine clinical care. Procedures All ERPDs were performed by endoscopists with over 10 years of ERCP experience. Under conscious sedation or general anesthesia, a duodenoscope (TJF-240/260, Olympus, Japan) was advanced to the descending duodenum. The papilla was cannulated with a sphincterotome or cannula directed toward the 1 to 2 o’ clock position to achieve selective access to the pancreatic duct. Pancreatography was performed to assess the site and extent of ductal disruption, communication with pancreatic fluid collections (PFCs), and the presence of proximal strictures. When strictures were identified, ductal dilation was carried out. Depending on accessibility, a stent or nasopancreatic drainage (NPD) catheter was placed across the leak, adjacent to the leak, or within the cavity. The type of drainage, as well as stent length and diameter, was determined at the discretion of the endoscopist. After the procedure, all patients underwent fasting and received acid suppression, prophylactic antibiotics, and intravenous fluid resuscitation, with close monitoring for signs of post-ERCP complications. Follow-up was scheduled at 1, 3, and 6 months post-procedure. For patients with nasopancreatic drainage, the catheter was removed after pancreatography confirmed fistula closure. In patients with stents, stent replacement was performed every 3 months until ERCP confirmed leak/fistula closure. No artificial intelligence or machine-learning tools were used in data collection or image interpretation. Definitions and outcomes The primary outcome was clinical success, defined as complete symptom resolution and radiologic improvement within 3 months, without the need for additional drainage or surgery. For patients with PFCs, success was defined as a reduction in PFC size to < 3 cm or at least a 50% decrease from baseline. For patients with an abdominal drain, success was defined as cessation of drainage and successful removal of the drain. Secondary outcomes included technical success, complication rate, timing of ERCP and stent indwelling time. Technical success was defined as successful cannulation of the pancreatic duct and stent placement. Adverse events were classified according to ASGE guidelines [ ].The Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI) was used to quantitatively assess patients’ comorbid conditions [ ]. Postoperative pancreatic fistula was defined according to the 2016 ISGPS update as drain amylase > 3× the upper limit of normal (ULN) [ ]. Pancreatitis-related duct leak/fistula was diagnosed by drain amylase > 3× ULN (if drained) or CT/MRI/MRCP findings suggestive of duct disruption (if not drained) and confirmed by ERCP showing contrast extravasation when endoscopic therapy was planned [ ]. Pancreatic fistulas were classified according to the endoscopy-oriented system [ ]. Type I involves parenchymal injury with leakage from small side branches or the distal main duct (IH: head; IB: body; IT: tail). Type II fistulas represent main pancreatic duct disruption (i.e., disrupted or disconnected duct syndrome) and were categorized as IIO (open proximal stump) or IIC (closed or obstructed proximal stump). Type III fistulas occur after pancreatic

by drain amylase > 3× ULN (if drained) or CT/MRI/MRCP findings suggestive of duct disruption (if not drained) and confirmed by ERCP showing contrast extravasation when endoscopic therapy was planned [ ]. Pancreatic fistulas were classified according to the endoscopy-oriented system [ ]. Type I involves parenchymal injury with leakage from small side branches or the distal main duct (IH: head; IB: body; IT: tail). Type II fistulas represent main pancreatic duct disruption (i.e., disrupted or disconnected duct syndrome) and were categorized as IIO (open proximal stump) or IIC (closed or obstructed proximal stump). Type III fistulas occur after pancreatic resection and were subclassified as IIIP (leak from the proximal remnant after distal pancreatectomy) or IIID (anastomotic leak after pancreaticoduodenectomy) (Fig. ). Drainage strategies for pancreatic fistulas were classified into three types. Type A places the stent across the fistula or leak. Type B places the stent near, but not within, the fistula or leak. Type C places the stent directly into the fluid collection cavity (Fig. ). Statistical analysis Continuous variables were tested for normality with the Shapiro–Wilk test and are reported as mean ± SD or median (IQR), as appropriate. Categorical variables are presented as frequencies and percentages. Group comparisons were performed using the t test or Mann–Whitney U test for continuous variables and the χ² or Fisher’s exact test for categorical variables. Trends in clinical success across drainage types were assessed with the Cochran–Armitage trend test. Variables with P < 0.10 in univariate analyses were entered into multivariable logistic regression to identify independent predictors of clinical success. Fistula classification was dichotomized (type IIC vs. non-IIC) for regression modeling. Odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were reported. Statistical analyses were performed using SPSS 26.0 and R 4.2.0, with two-sided P < 0.05 considered significant. Results Baseline characteristics A total of 106 patients with pancreatic fistula were enrolled (74 men, 32 women; mean age 49.4 ± 15.9 years). The mean BMI was 22.0 ± 3.6 kg/m², and the median CCI was 3 (IQR 1–5); 14 patients (13.2%) had diabetes. Etiologies included pancreatitis in 71 patients (67.0%)—comprising 50 acute (47.2%) and 21 chronic cases (19.8%)—postoperative leaks in 31 (29.2%) (partial pancreatectomy/enucleation, 19 [17.9%]; distal pancreatectomy, 12 [11.3%]), and trauma in 4 (3.8%). Peripancreatic fluid collections were present in 83 patients (78.3%), including 65 pancreatic pseudocysts (61.3%) and 18 cases of walled-off necrosis (17.0%). Fifty-three patients (50.0%) had an abdominal drain in place before ERCP. Baseline demographic and clinical data are summarized in Table . Outcomes A total of 168 ERCP sessions were performed (median 1 [IQR 1–2] per patient). The median procedure time was 35.5 min (IQR 21.0–52.8), and the median interval from diagnosis to ERCP was 68.5 days (IQR 23.0–160.0). Technical success was 98.2% (165/168), while overall clinical success was 79.2% (84/106). Three ERCP sessions were technically unsuccessful because proximal pancreatic duct strictures prevented stent deployment. These patients subsequently underwent scheduled repeat ERCP, and technical success was achieved after pancreatic duct dilation. Of the 22 patients classified as clinical failures, 8 underwent additional endoscopic management (EUS-guided transmural drainage, n = 4; direct endoscopic necrosectomy, n = 4), 12 required additional surgical management, and 2 died. Fistula locations included head (23.6%, 25/106), neck (15.1%, 16/106), body (19.8%, 21/106), and tail (41.5%, 44/106). Stents of 7 Fr (52.8%) and 5 Fr (44.3%) were most commonly used. The majority of patients (91.5%) underwent single-stent drainage; 8 patients (7.5%) received two stents and 1 patient (0.9%) received three. Among patients with type IIC fistulas, conversion to type IIO was achieved in 5 cases following pancreatic duct dilation. The clinical success rate was comparable between pancreatitis-related fistulas (78.9%) and postoperative/traumatic fistulas (80.0%) ( P = 0.893). Drainage type, fistula site, proximal duct stricture, and number of ERCP sessions did not differ significantly between groups ( P > 0.05). Etiology-based outcomes were summarized in Table . Predictors of clinical success A total of 15 variables were analyzed for their association with clinical success. In univariate analysis, classification and drainage methods were significantly associated with clinical success (Table ). In contrast, variables such as the timing of ERCP and etiology were not associated with clinical success. In an exploratory analysis restricted to pancreatitis-related cases, clinical success did not differ significantly between acute and chronic pancreatitis (38/50 [76.0%] vs. 18/21 [85.7%], Fisher’s exact P = 0.527). Leak-bridging drainage was associated with a higher success rate (94.4%, 34/36) compared to non-leak-bridging drainage (71.4%, 50/70). Success rates by classification were as follows: type IH (100%, 9/9), type IB (100%, 4/4), type IT (100%, 6/6), type IIO (79.7%, 51/64), type IIC (36.4%, 4/11), and type IIIP (83.3%, 10/12). Type IIC had the lowest success rate (36.4%, 4/11) compared to non-IIC fistulas (81.1%, 77/95). Classification was dichotomized into IIC versus non-IIC for multivariate analysis. Variables with P < 0.1

Leak-bridging drainage was associated with a higher success rate (94.4%, 34/36) compared to non-leak-bridging drainage (71.4%, 50/70). Success rates by classification were as follows: type IH (100%, 9/9), type IB (100%, 4/4), type IT (100%, 6/6), type IIO (79.7%, 51/64), type IIC (36.4%, 4/11), and type IIIP (83.3%, 10/12). Type IIC had the lowest success rate (36.4%, 4/11) compared to non-IIC fistulas (81.1%, 77/95). Classification was dichotomized into IIC versus non-IIC for multivariate analysis. Variables with P < 0.1 in univariate analysis were entered into the multivariable logistic regression model. Multivariable analysis identified leak-bridging drainage (OR 6.5, 95% CI 1.3–31.2; P = 0.020) as an independent positive predictor of clinical success, whereas type IIC fistulas were independently associated with lower odds of success (OR 0.114, 95% CI 0.027–0.476; P = 0.003). Drainage method analysis The clinical success rates were 94.4% (34/36) for type A, 83.3% (35/42) for type B, and 53.6% (15/28) for type C (χ² test, P < 0.001). A significant decreasing trend in clinical success was observed from type A to type C (Cochran–Armitage trend test, P < 0.001). In the non–type A subgroup, type B was associated with a higher success rate than type C (83.3% [35/42] vs. 53.6% [15/28]; χ² test, P = 0.007). Adverse events and follow-up ERCP-related adverse events occurred in 9 patients (8.5%), including 7 cases of post-ERCP pancreatitis (PEP) (6.6%) and 2 deaths (1.9%). All seven cases of PEP improved with conservative management. One patient died of respiratory failure due to pancreatopleural fistula, and the other died of septic shock secondary to infected WON. During a median follow-up of 20.9 months (IQR 9.3–40.6), stent-related adverse events occurred in 8 patients (7.5%). Three patients developed stent occlusion, presenting with increased abdominal drain output; all were managed with repeat ERCP and stent exchange, achieving clinical success. Stent dislodgement was detected in 5 patients during follow-up: 3 were asymptomatic with no contrast extravasation on repeat pancreatography and therefore did not require stent replacement, whereas 2 underwent repeat ERCP with repeat stent placement and achieved clinical success. Eighteen patients (17.0%) developed new-onset diabetes during follow-up. The median stent indwelling time was 163.5 days (IQR 79.5–291.3), after which the stents were removed. Discussion Pancreatic leaks and fistulas are serious complications of pancreatitis, pancreatic surgery, or trauma. In this multicenter retrospective cohort, ERPD achieved high technical and clinical success, with a clinical success rate of 79.2%, which is consistent with previously reported rates of 71% to 92% [ , , ]. Leak-bridging drainage independently predicted treatment success, whereas type IIC fistula was strongly associated with lower odds of success. When leak-bridging drainage was not feasible, stent placement adjacent to the leak was more effective than intracavitary drainage. Although ERCP has been used to treat pancreatic leaks and fistulas for decades, its effectiveness—especially for pancreatitis-related leaks—remains controversial [ , ]. Several studies have suggested that outcomes are less favorable in pancreatitis, with reported success rates as low as 55% [ , ]. A commonly proposed explanation is the inability to bridge the site of ductal disruption and thereby re-establish ductal continuity. Das et al. [ ] observed higher success in non–acute pancreatitis than in acute pancreatitis (90.3% vs. 68.6%), whereas Chen et al. [ ] reported similar outcomes between pancreatitis-associated disconnected duct syndrome and trauma-related injury (71.4% vs. 66.7%). Among pancreatitis-related leaks, success was numerically lower in acute than chronic pancreatitis (76.0% vs. 85.7%), but not statistically significant. Success did not differ between pancreatitis-related and postoperative/traumatic leaks (78.9% vs. 80.0%; P = 0.893), supporting similar effectiveness of ERPD across etiologies. Mutignani et al. [ ] proposed an endoscopy-oriented classification of pancreatic fistulas, which we further evaluated in our cohort. Type I fistulas had favorable outcomes, with a clinical success rate of 100%. In contrast, type IIC fistulas had a markedly lower success rate (36.4%, 4/11). Management of type IIC lesions is technically challenging because effective therapy often requires access to the distal pancreatic duct. This typically involves puncturing and dilating the closed stump to convert a type IIC lesion into a type IIO leak, followed by bridging the leak with a stent, or alternatively decompressing distal pancreatic secretions using a transpapillary stent [ ]. When conversion to a type IIO leak is not feasible, additional EUS-guided transmural drainage may be required to achieve clinical resolution [ – ]. In our cohort, leak-bridging drainage was associated with higher clinical success than non–leak-bridging drainage, consistent with prior studies [ , , , ]. The likely mechanism is that transpapillary or transfistulous stenting bridges the site of ductal disruption, facilitates drainage of pancreatic juice into the duodenum, lowers intraductal pressure, and thereby promotes fistula closure [ , , ]. When complete

leak with a stent, or alternatively decompressing distal pancreatic secretions using a transpapillary stent [ ]. When conversion to a type IIO leak is not feasible, additional EUS-guided transmural drainage may be required to achieve clinical resolution [ – ]. In our cohort, leak-bridging drainage was associated with higher clinical success than non–leak-bridging drainage, consistent with prior studies [ , , , ]. The likely mechanism is that transpapillary or transfistulous stenting bridges the site of ductal disruption, facilitates drainage of pancreatic juice into the duodenum, lowers intraductal pressure, and thereby promotes fistula closure [ , , ]. When complete disruption of the pancreatic duct occurs, leak-bridging drainage is technically challenging [ ]. Ge et.al [ ] described intracavitary stent placement (type C) as an option in selected cases. In our study, type C drainage was less effective than type B drainage. One possible explanation is that intracavitary stenting may impede physiologic pancreatic outflow and thereby hinder fistula healing; in addition, the small caliber of pancreatic stents may predispose to occlusion, particularly in the presence of intracavitary necrotic debris, which can further increase intracavitary pressure and delay closure. These findings suggest that when leak-bridging drainage is not feasible, intracavitary drainage (type C) may be less preferable than stent placement adjacent to the leak (type B). This study has several limitations. Its retrospective design is subject to selection bias and residual confounding, and management was not protocolized, with the drainage strategy, including selective use of a NPD versus stenting, left to the endoscopist’s discretion. In addition, techniques, devices, and supportive care likely evolved over the 16-year study period, and follow-up was not standardized across centers, which may affect estimates of longer-term outcomes and recurrence. Conclusions In summary, ERPD is a safe and effective treatment for pancreatic leaks and fistulas. Leak-bridging drainage should be prioritized whenever technically feasible, as it is strongly associated with higher clinical success; when bridging cannot be achieved, stent placement adjacent to the leak appears to be more effective than intracavitary drainage. Type IIC fistulas have substantially lower success rates with ERPD and may require additional or adjunctive interventions, such as EUS-guided drainage.

documents.title: ASGE Guideline Role of EUS in the Evaluation of Pancreatic Cysts and Solid Lesions

chunks.content: Introduction Gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GISTs) represent the most prevalent mesenchymal neoplasms of the gastrointestinal tract, with gastric GISTs accounting for the majority of cases , . Small gastric GISTs, defined as tumors with a diameter < 2.0 cm, constitute a distinct subgroup that, despite their relatively indolent biological behavior in most instances, retains malignant potential and carries a non-negligible risk of metastasis . Epidemiological evidence from the SEER database underscores this concern: among 378 patients with newly diagnosed GISTs, 11.4% presented with local progression or distant metastasis at initial diagnosis, with these patients exhibiting a significantly elevated 5-year cause-specific mortality rate compared to those without metastasis . These findings align with consensus guidelines from European and Japanese experts, which advocate surgical resection for all pathologically confirmed GISTs, irrespective of tumor size, to mitigate the risk of disease progression , . Consequently, the accurate preoperative differentiation of small gastric GISTs from other gastric submucosal tumors (SMTs) is paramount for guiding optimal clinical management. Endoscopic ultrasonography (EUS) has emerged as the premier imaging modality for the initial assessment and characterization of gastric SMTs, providing high-resolution visualization of tumor size, location, layer of origin, echogenic patterns, and morphological features—parameters critical for distinguishing benign from malignant lesions , , . However, the diagnostic utility of EUS is constrained by the overlapping imaging characteristics of GISTs and benign SMTs, particularly leiomyomas, which frequently complicate traditional radiological interpretation . Prior studies report that EUS alone achieves a diagnostic accuracy of approximately 70% for GISTs, with performance further diminished in small gastric GISTs due to their subtle and often atypical imaging features . To address these limitations, recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) have introduced deep learning-based systems that demonstrate remarkable capabilities in analyzing EUS images to differentiate GISTs from benign lesions, including leiomyomas. These models have shown superior accuracy compared to human readers in certain studies, highlighting their potential to enhance clinical decision-making. Emerging research even suggests their potential for direct risk stratification, which could further optimize treatment strategies – . However, it is important to acknowledge that while AI models offer significant promise, they also face challenges. One key limitation is the inherent “black box” nature of some systems, which renders their decision-making processes inscrutable to clinicians and may limit trust in their outputs . Additionally, existing AI frameworks often process EUS images in isolation, potentially neglecting essential clinical context—such as patient demographics, symptoms, or endoscopist observations—that could influence diagnostic certainty. These gaps highlight the need for a more transparent, clinically integrated approach to preoperative GIST diagnosis. In this study, we aimed to develop and validate a novel, reproducible, and clinically applicable EUS-based risk-scoring system that synergizes key endoscopic ultrasonography imaging biomarkers to enhance the accuracy and interpretability of small gastric GIST diagnosis. By leveraging standardized EUS-derived characteristics, this tool seeks to provide clinicians with a practical, evidence-based framework for preoperative risk stratification and informed personalized treatment decisions for gastric SMTs. Materials and methods Patients This retrospective investigation examined medical records of individuals presenting with upper gastrointestinal manifestations who received gastroscopic and EUS examinations across several medical institutions from January 2015 to December 2024. All EUS examinations were performed by experienced endoscopists with a minimum of 5 years of dedicated EUS practice, each having performed over 500 diagnostic EUS procedures, using an ultrasound mini-probe (Olympus, Japan) with a standard frequency of 12 MHz. The EUS characteristics of the gastric SMTs were assessed based on standardized EUS reports and corresponding ultrasound images. Eligible participants met the following conditions: (1) gastroscopic and EUS confirmation of gastric SMTs; (2) lesion diameter below 2.0 cm; and (3) receipt of endoscopic intervention. Cases were excluded based on the following: (1) SMT measurements of 2.0 cm or larger; (2) absence of surgical management; (3) ambiguous pathological findings; or (4) insufficient clinical documentation. For analysis, subjects from the First Affiliated Hospital of Soochow University were randomly assigned to either a training cohort (TC, n = 670) or an internal validation cohort (IVC, n = 287) at a ratio of 7:3. Additionally, patients from Nanjing First Hospital, Changshu Hospital Affiliated to Soochow University, the Affiliated Zhangjiagang Hospital of Soochow University, and No.1 People’s Hospital of Kunshan were collectively designated as the external validation cohort (EVC), comprising 346 cases. The study design is summarized in Fig. . The research protocol received ethical approval from the Institutional Review Board of Changshu Hospital Affiliated to Soochow University (Approval No: L2025055), which served as the central ethics committee for this multi-center study, with additional approvals obtained from the local ethics committees of all other participating institutions. Written informed consent was obtained from all participants. All methods were performed in accordance with the relevant guidelines and regulations. Quality control in multicenter data and pathology To ensure consistency and reliability across multiple centers, stringent quality control measures were implemented.

The research protocol received ethical approval from the Institutional Review Board of Changshu Hospital Affiliated to Soochow University (Approval No: L2025055), which served as the central ethics committee for this multi-center study, with additional approvals obtained from the local ethics committees of all other participating institutions. Written informed consent was obtained from all participants. All methods were performed in accordance with the relevant guidelines and regulations. Quality control in multicenter data and pathology To ensure consistency and reliability across multiple centers, stringent quality control measures were implemented. First, a pathological review was conducted for all cases. Specifically, pathological specimens and diagnostic reports from each participating institution were re-assessed independently by two experienced gastrointestinal pathologists, who were blinded to the original diagnoses and patient groupings. Discrepancies were resolved through joint discussion to establish a final consensus diagnosis. Second, a standardized operating procedure for EUS examination and image interpretation was developed and distributed to all involved endoscopists. Finally, a dedicated data management team performed periodic audits of the submitted clinical and EUS data, checking for missing values, outliers, and logical inconsistencies. While formal statistical analysis of intra- and inter-observer agreement (e.g., Kappa values) for EUS features like echogenicity was not performed in this retrospective design, several steps were taken to promote consistent interpretation and data quality across centers. These included the implementation of standardized operating procedures and centralized data audits, as described above. A formal assessment of observer variability is planned for the prospective validation phase of this scoring system to further establish the reliability of these key EUS characteristics. Data collection The data collected in this study included the following variables: gender, age, tumor location, presence of surface ulceration, tumor growth pattern, layer of origin as determined by EUS, echogenic features (including echogenicity and homogeneity), lesion morphology, margin demarcation, and postoperative pathological results. All EUS examinations were performed by experienced endoscopists. The EUS characteristics of the gastric SMTs were assessed based on standardized EUS reports and corresponding ultrasound images. Definitions Tumor size was measured by EUS. Based on the morphological characteristics observed during EUS examination, the tumors were classified as either regular (demonstrating round, oval, or nodular shapes) or irregular (exhibiting a branching or lobulated structure). Growth pattern was defined as intraluminal if more than 50% of the tumor was located within the gastric wall, and extraluminal if more than 50% extended beyond the gastric wall , . For the assessment of echogenicity, lesions with mixed or heterogeneous echo patterns were classified based on the predominant (> 50%) echo pattern observed. If no single pattern predominated, the lesion was categorized as having medium echogenicity. For the purpose of this study, a “small gastric GIST” was defined as a lesion with a maximum diameter of less than 2.0 cm as measured by EUS, with the diagnosis subsequently confirmed by postoperative histopathological examination and positive immunohistochemical staining for CD117 (c-KIT), CD34, and/or DOG-1. Statistical analysis When presenting categorical data, we utilized frequencies and proportions, and employed the Chi-square test for comparing differences between groups. To distinguish between small gastric stromal tumors and non-small gastric stromal tumors, univariate analysis was performed first. Variables demonstrating statistical significance ( P < 0.05) in the univariate analysis were subsequently incorporated into a multiple logistic regression framework. A stepwise selection method (both forward and backward) was employed to identify the final independent predictors, using the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) as the stopping rule. Before constructing the final model, multicollinearity among the candidate variables was assessed using the variance inflation factor (VIF), with a VIF value of less than 5 indicating no significant collinearity. The scoring system was then constructed by standardizing the regression coefficients (β values) derived from the final multivariate model. The variable with the smallest absolute β coefficient was chosen as the reference (assigned a score of 1), and the scores for the remaining variables were determined proportionally based on the ratios of their coefficients, with the results rounded to the nearest whole number. For model validation, two separate analytical approaches were adopted: discrimination was evaluated through receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis, with the area under the curve (AUC) calculated for quantification , goodness-of-fit was assessed using calibration plots, and clinical utility estimation through decision curve analysis (DCA). To gauge model performance, diagnostic accuracy indicators were computed, encompassing sensitivity, specificity, overall accuracy, positive predictive value (PPV), and negative predictive value (NPV). The primary endpoint of this study was the discriminative performance of the developed risk-scoring system for the preoperative diagnosis of small gastric GISTs, assessed by the AUC. Secondary endpoints included sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV, overall accuracy, calibration, and clinical utility. All computational tasks were executed using the R statistical computing environment (version 4.1.0), with the significance threshold (α) set at 0.05
