Results Baseline characteristics of patients A total of 1303 patients were enrolled in this study, comprising 670 in the TC, 287 in the IVC, and 346 in the EVC. The number of gastric stromal tumor cases was 300 in the TC, 128 in the IVC, and 186 in the EVC, respectively. Table summarizes the baseline characteristics of patients in the TC and IVC. No statistically significant differences were observed between these two cohorts ( P > 0.05), demonstrating their comparability. The median tumor size across all cohorts was consistent, measuring 1.5 cm (interquartile range (IQR): 1.0–1.8) in the TC, 1.5 cm (IQR: 1.1–1.8) in the IVC, and 1.4 cm (IQR: 1.0–1.8) in the EVC. Figure displays white-light endoscopic and EUS features of six distinct types of gastric SMTs. Figure presents the distribution of gastric stromal tumors versus non-stromal tumors in the TC according to tumor location, layer of origin, growth pattern, and echogenicity. Supplementary Fig. 1 and Supplementary Fig. 2 show the corresponding distributions of these four characteristics in the IVC and EVC, respectively. Supplementary Table 1 provides the baseline characteristics of patients in the TC and EVC. Significant differences were identified between these groups in terms of pathological type and age ( P < 0.05), whereas other baseline characteristics showed no significant differences ( P > 0.05). Comparison of characteristics between small gastric stromal tumor group and non-small gastric stromal tumor group Based on postoperative pathological findings, gastric SMTs were classified into gastric stromal tumors and non-gastric stromal tumors. In the TC, gastric stromal tumors occurred most frequently in the gastric cardia/fundus (57.7%), with the vast majority (84.7%) arising from the muscularis propria layer. Most lesions (81.0%) appeared hypoechoic. Additionally, compared to non-gastric stromal tumors, a significantly higher proportion of gastric stromal tumors showed extraluminal growth (22.3% vs. 3.2%). Supplementary Table 2 compares the clinical and EUS features between gastric stromal tumors and non-stromal tumors in the IVC, indicating significant differences in tumor location, layer of origin, growth pattern, and echogenicity ( P < 0.05). Similarly, in the EVC, these four characteristics also differed significantly between the two groups ( P < 0.05), as detailed in Supplementary Table 3. Supplementary Table 4 presents the distribution of non-small gastric stromal tumors across the three cohorts. Risk factors for predicting gastric submucosal tumors as gastric stromal tumors and the development of a scoring system model In the TC, univariate analysis identified tumor location, layer of origin, growth pattern, and echogenicity as risk factors for predicting gastric stromal tumors among gastric SMTs (Table ). Multivariate analysis confirmed these four characteristics as independent predictors (Table ). Specifically, SMTs located in the cardia/fundus carried a significantly higher risk of being classified as gastric stromal tumors compared to those in the gastric body (OR = 2.96, 95% CI: 1.96–4.63, P < 0.001). Tumors originating from the MP were more likely to be gastric stromal tumors than those from the MM/SM (OR = 8.80, 95% CI: 5.80-13.66, P < 0.001). Hypoechoic lesions on EUS had a higher risk than those with medium/high echogenicity (OR = 2.65, 95% CI: 1.74–4.08, P < 0.001), and tumors with extraluminal growth were more likely to be stromal tumors than those with intraluminal growth (OR = 8.65, 95% CI: 4.33–18.71, P < 0.001). Based on the β-coefficients from the multivariate analysis, each risk factor was assigned a score: tumor location (cardia/fundus: 1 point; gastric body/antrum: 0 points), layer of origin (MP: 2 points; MM/SM: 0 points), echogenicity (low: 1 points; medium/high: 0 points), and growth pattern (extraluminal: 2 points; intraluminal: 0 points) (Table ). The cutoff score of ≥ 3 was chosen based on clinical interpretability and risk stratification, corresponding to the intermediate- and high-risk categories for suspected GISTs. Validation of the scoring system In the TC, the proportion of gastric stromal tumors increased with higher risk scores: 8.5% (score 0), 9.4% , 30.4% , 55.6% , 76.5% , 96.4% , and 100.0% (Fig. ). The scoring system achieved an AUC of 0.838 (95% CI: 0.808–0.867; Fig. A), reflecting strong discriminative performance. Good agreement between predictions and observations was indicated by the calibration curve ( P > 0.05; Fig. D). In the TC, the DCA curve analysis

of ≥ 3 was chosen based on clinical interpretability and risk stratification, corresponding to the intermediate- and high-risk categories for suspected GISTs. Validation of the scoring system In the TC, the proportion of gastric stromal tumors increased with higher risk scores: 8.5% (score 0), 9.4% , 30.4% , 55.6% , 76.5% , 96.4% , and 100.0% (Fig. ). The scoring system achieved an AUC of 0.838 (95% CI: 0.808–0.867; Fig. A), reflecting strong discriminative performance. Good agreement between predictions and observations was indicated by the calibration curve ( P > 0.05; Fig. D). In the TC, the DCA curve analysis of the scoring system showed that when the predicted threshold probability for small gastric GISTs fell within the range of 20% to 70%, clinical interventions could achieve a net benefit of approximately 33% (Fig. G). Diagnostic metrics included a sensitivity of 0.833, specificity of 0.708, accuracy of 0.764, PPV of 0.698, and NPV of 0.840 (Table ). Based on score ranges, risk categories were defined as low (0–2; 16.0%), intermediate (3–4; 64.9%), and high (5–6; 98.1%) (Fig. ). Within the IVC, a progressive increase in gastric stromal tumor incidence was observed across ascending scores: 3.7% (score 1), 22.5% , 44.9% , 67.9% , 93.8% , and 100.0% (Fig. ). The model yielded an AUC of 0.776 (95% CI: 0.727–0.826; Fig. B), demonstrating acceptable discrimination. Calibration performance was satisfactory, with no significant deviation from ideal predictions ( P > 0.05; Fig. E). The DCA curve (Fig. H) shows that when the threshold probability of small gastric GISTs predicted by the scoring system is within the 20%-60% range, implementing interventions can achieve a net benefit of approximately 33%. The system showed a sensitivity of 0.867, specificity of 0.509, accuracy of 0.669, PPV of 0.587, and NPV of 0.827 (Table ). Tumor rates by risk category were 17.3% (low), 52.8% (intermediate), and 96.2% (high) (Fig. ). In the EVC, gastric stromal tumor prevalence also correlated positively with assigned scores: 3.4% (score 0), 18.0% , 33.9% , 65.1% , 84.5% , and 95.0% (both scores 5 and 6) (Fig. ). The AUC was 0.844 (95% CI: 0.805–0.884; Fig. C), indicating high discriminatory power. Calibration was accurate, with good alignment between predicted and observed outcomes ( P > 0.05; Fig. F). A net benefit of 40% was observed for interventions when the predicted probability of small gastric GISTs was between 20% and 80%, according to the DCA (Fig. I). Performance measures included sensitivity of 0.828, specificity of 0.731, accuracy of 0.783, PPV of 0.782, and NPV of 0.785 (Table ). Stratification into risk groups revealed tumor rates of 21.5% (low), 73.9% (intermediate), and 95.0% (high) (Fig. ). Discussion In this study, we developed and rigorously validated a novel EUS-based risk-scoring system that integrates critical endoscopic and clinical characteristics to facilitate the preoperative differentiation of small gastric GISTs from other SMTs. The model, constructed using four independent predictors—tumor location in the cardia/fundus, origin within the muscularis propria, hypoechoic echogenicity, and extraluminal growth pattern—demonstrated strong diagnostic performance in both internal and external validation cohorts, with AUC values of 0.776 and 0.844, respectively. This scoring system enables effective risk stratification, where high-risk scores (5–6 points) are strongly associated with GIST diagnosis, underscoring its potential utility in guiding preoperative decision-making and optimizing treatment strategies for gastric SMTs. EUS remains the most widely utilized modality for the diagnosis of GISTs due to its ability to clearly visualize key features such as tumor location, layer of origin, echogenicity, morphology, and growth pattern , . However, previous studies have highlighted its limitations in distinguishing GISTs from other mesenchymal tumors, such as leiomyomas and schwannomas, often necessitating histopathological confirmation – . For instance, Iwahashi et al. reported that EUS exhibited a sensitivity of 83.3% and specificity of 66.7% for diagnosing gastric stromal tumors, with sensitivity dropping to 73.3% for tumors smaller than 3 cm. Although EUS-guided fine-needle aspiration (EUS-FNA) is a standard tool for evaluating gastric SMTs and enables ultrasound-guided sampling for pathological diagnosis, it has several drawbacks, including limited specimen yield, risk of false-negative results, technical complexity, high operator dependency, and potential complications such as tumor rupture and peritoneal seeding , . The diagnostic performance of EUS-FNA is particularly suboptimal for gastric SMTs smaller than 2.0 cm , . In contrast, contrast-enhanced harmonic EUS (CEH-EUS) offers a less invasive alternative, minimizing patient trauma and procedure-related risks while facilitating real-time assessment of enhancement patterns and dynamic microvascular perfusion, which aids in distinguishing malignant-potential GISTs from benign SMTs , . Nonetheless, according to the American College of Gastroenterology (ACG) clinical guidelines, CEH-EUS also has limited diagnostic value for sub-2 cm GISTs . A meta-analysis of four studies involving 187 patients with SMTs who underwent contrast-enhanced EUS reported diagnostic sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy of 89%, 82%, and 89%, respectively, for GISTs . Nonetheless, according to the American College of Gastroenterology (ACG) clinical guidelines, CEH-EUS also has limited diagnostic value for sub-2 cm GISTs . A meta-analysis of four studies involving 187 patients with SMTs who underwent contrast-enhanced EUS reported diagnostic sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy of 89%, 82%, and 89%, respectively, for GISTs . It is important to contextualize the performance of our EUS-based scoring system (sensitivity: 0.867 and NPV: 0.827 in the IVC) against these modalities. While the specificity of our model is lower than that reported for CEH-EUS, its strength lies in its high sensitivity and, most notably, its high NPV. This performance profile is particularly suited for a ‘rule-out’ clinical strategy. A high NPV means that a low-risk score can reliably identify lesions that are unlikely to be GISTs, potentially helping to avoid unnecessary invasive diagnostic procedures or treatments for a substantial subset of patients with benign SMTs. Therefore, our simple scoring system and CEH-EUS may serve complementary roles: the former as an accessible, initial triage tool to identify low-risk lesions, and the latter as a more advanced, albeit less widely available, technique for further characterizing indeterminate or high-risk cases. Despite the improved accuracy achieved with contrast agents, over 10% of cases remain indeterminate, and the use of contrast carries inherent risks. Collectively, these limitations underscore the persistent clinical need for reliable non-invasive methods to accurately differentiate small gastric SMTs. Scoring systems serve as widely adopted quantitative tools in medical research, integrating multidimensional clinical and biological parameters to offer an objective foundation for disease diagnosis, risk stratification, prognosis estimation, and treatment planning. By transforming subjective or intricate assessments into quantifiable scores or categories, they facilitate scientific decision-making, evaluation, and comparative analysis. In a multicenter retrospective study, He et al. identified risk factors associated with intraoperative perforation during endoscopic resection of gastric stromal tumors and established a scoring model that exhibited strong predictive accuracy in both IVC and EVC, offering clinicians an efficient and practical tool for procedural planning. Similarly, a difficulty scoring system previously developed by our research team also demonstrated robust predictive performance in preoperatively assessing challenges in endoscopic resection of gastric stromal tumors . In the diagnostic evaluation of gastric SMTs, accurately distinguishing GISTs—which carry malignant potential—from non-GIST lesions is of critical importance. This study identified four independent predictive factors for gastric GISTs: location in the cardia/fundus, origin within the muscularis propria, hypoechoic echogenicity, and extraluminal growth pattern. We observed that gastric GISTs occurred predominantly in the cardia and fundus, whereas non-GIST SMTs were more frequently located in the gastric body and antrum. This distribution is consistent with previous reports – and may be attributed to differences in embryonic origin, local tissue microenvironment, and anatomicophysiological features. The cardia and fundus, derived from the foregut, harbor a high density of interstitial cells of Cajal (ICC)—the cell of origin for GISTs—or their precursors. The thicker muscularis layer and distinct neurovascular supply in this region may further support GIST development. In contrast, the gastric body and antrum are characterized by heightened mechanical stress and acid exposure, which may favor the development of other SMTs. The exact mechanisms underlying this anatomic predilection, however, require further elucidation. The origin of GISTs within the MP reflects their fundamental biology and serves as a key diagnostic discriminator. As GISTs typically arise from ICCs, which are predominantly located within the muscularis propria, this layer represents the most common site of tumor initiation. EUS studies have consistently shown that a muscularis propria origin is strongly associated with GIST diagnosis, likely due to the permissive stromal environment that facilitates tumor growth and invasion. This site specificity may also relate to molecular markers characteristic of ICCs, such as DOG1 expression , . Furthermore, our results confirm that hypoechoic appearance on EUS is a typical feature of GISTs, which can be explained by their histologic composition. The tumors are composed of densely packed, homogeneous cells with hypervascular stroma and scant fibrous tissue, leading to reduced ultrasound reflection and lower echogenicity. Acoustic impedance differences between the tumor and adjacent normal layers may also contribute to this sonographic pattern. Additionally, we found that GISTs accounted for a significantly higher proportion of SMTs with extraluminal growth compared to non-GIST subtypes. This growth pattern aligns with the aggressive biological behavior and anatomic origin of GISTs. Arising from the muscularis propria, GIST cells often exhibit infiltrative growth, penetrating muscle layers and expanding outward toward the subserosa and peritoneal cavity—areas of lower mechanical resistance. Additionally, we found that GISTs accounted for a significantly higher proportion of SMTs with extraluminal growth compared to non-GIST subtypes. This growth pattern aligns with the aggressive biological behavior and anatomic origin of GISTs. Arising from the muscularis propria, GIST cells often exhibit infiltrative growth, penetrating muscle layers and expanding outward toward the subserosa and peritoneal cavity—areas of lower mechanical resistance. This directional tendency may also be influenced by tumor vascularization and adaptive interactions with the local microenvironment. In contrast, most benign SMTs (e.g., leiomyomas or lipomas) typically demonstrate slow growth confined to the gastric wall or intraluminal protrusion, seldom showing extraluminal extension. Our study identified four independent predictors—location in the cardia/fundus, origin within the muscularis propria, hypoechoic echogenicity, and extraluminal growth pattern—while other EUS features such as irregular margins, lesion morphology, and the presence of surface ulceration, which were also collected and analyzed, were not retained in the final model. This contrasts with some previous studies that have suggested a potential role for features like irregular borders or ulceration in diagnosing GISTs , . The discrepancy may be attributable to several factors specific to our study cohort. First, the inclusion was restricted to small gastric SMTs (< 2 cm), among which malignant features like irregular margins or ulceration might be less developed or apparent compared to larger lesions. Second, in the context of small tumors, the four identified predictors may represent more fundamental and dominant characteristics related to the origin and intrinsic biology of GISTs, potentially overshadowing the contribution of other morphological features in multivariate analysis. Furthermore, the high collinearity between certain features (e.g., an extraluminal growth pattern and irregular borders) might have resulted in only the strongest independent predictor being selected. While the omission of these other features could be perceived as a limitation, the robust performance of our parsimonious model across validation cohorts suggests that the selected four variables capture the most critical discriminatory information for small gastric GISTs, supporting its utility as an effective and streamlined preoperative tool. Future studies incorporating larger lesions or additional imaging modalities might further elucidate the role of these other characteristics. Despite the promising performance of our risk-scoring system, several limitations should be acknowledged. First, the retrospective design and the inclusion of only resected lesions may introduce verification bias, as all analyzed tumors were confirmed pathologically following intervention. This could lead to an overestimation of the model’s sensitivity, since lesions that were not resected—and might have been false negatives—were not included. However, our scoring system is intended for clinical scenarios where resection is already under consideration, and its high negative predictive value may still offer utility in ruling out low-risk lesions within this context. Second, all EUS examinations were performed by experienced endoscopists, which may not reflect the variability in operator skill and experience across different clinical settings. Third, although the scoring system integrated key EUS and clinical features, other potential predictors such as contrast-enhanced EUS characteristics or molecular markers were not included. Future studies incorporating advanced imaging modalities and biomarker data may further improve diagnostic accuracy. Fourth, while our model aids in diagnosis, future iterations should aim to incorporate established risk criteria (such as mitotic count from biopsy specimens or enhanced imaging features) to predict the malignant potential of diagnosed GISTs and thus more directly guide treatment decisions. Fifth, it should be noted that the current model exhibits a performance trade-off characterized by high sensitivity and NPV but modest specificity. While this makes it an effective tool for ruling out GISTs, the relatively lower specificity could lead to false-positive results, potentially recommending further intervention for some benign lesions. The clinical utility of the model therefore rests on its application as a high-sensitivity screening and triage instrument. Sixth, our study did not incorporate advanced molecular imaging techniques such as EUS-elastography or contrast-enhanced EUS (CE-EUS), nor did it include a cost-effectiveness analysis of the proposed scoring system. Finally, the model was developed and validated in a Chinese population. Its applicability to other ethnic groups and healthcare settings (e.g., Western populations) remains to be evaluated. Differences in GIST prevalence, genetic backgrounds, endoscopist EUS experience, and technical equipment could potentially influence the performance and calibration of the scoring system. External validation in diverse, international cohorts is a necessary next step before widespread global adoption can be recommended. The proposed EUS-based risk-scoring system can be readily incorporated into existing diagnostic algorithms for small gastric subepithelial lesions, such as those recommended by the ACG guidelines. The proposed EUS-based risk-scoring system can be readily incorporated into existing diagnostic algorithms for small gastric subepithelial lesions, such as those recommended by the ACG guidelines. As a first-line triage tool following standard EUS examination, the scoring system can assist clinicians in stratifying lesions into low-, intermediate-, and high-risk categories. For low-risk lesions (score 0–2), a watchful waiting approach with periodic surveillance could be adopted, aligning with current recommendations for likely benign SMTs. Intermediate-risk lesions (score 3–4) may warrant further diagnostic evaluation, such as EUS-FNA or contrast-enhanced EUS, to clarify pathological diagnosis before deciding on resection. High-risk lesions (score 5–6) could be prioritized for endoscopic or surgical resection in accordance with guideline-based management of suspected GISTs. This stratified approach not only complements existing protocols but also provides a reproducible, quantitative framework to standardize decision-making across different clinical settings. In summary, we developed and validated a practical EUS-based risk-scoring system that effectively integrates tumor location, layer of origin, echogenicity, and growth pattern to preoperatively differentiate small gastric GISTs from other SMTs. The model demonstrated robust diagnostic performance and reliable risk stratification across both internal and external validation cohorts, offering a non-invasive, reproducible, and clinically applicable tool to support individualized treatment planning. While further prospective validation is warranted, this scoring system has the potential to enhance preoperative decision-making and optimize management strategies for patients with small gastric SMTs. chunks.content: Introduction The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into healthcare has attracted growing interest and research over the past decade [ ]. AI applications in medicine encompass a broad spectrum, including diagnostic algorithms and tools designed to enhance patient education. AI-driven chatbots have shown potential in enhancing patient communication and education [ ]. With the advent of more advanced AI models like OpenAI's ChatGPT-4.0, there is a growing curiosity about their utility in providing medical advice that aligns with established clinical guidelines. Pre-colonoscopy patient guidance is a critical aspect of gastrointestinal care. Accurate and comprehensible information regarding diet and medication management is essential for the success of the procedure [ ]. However, disseminating this information efficiently and effectively remains a challenge, often leading to patient misconceptions and non-compliance [ ]. While there has been considerable research on the use of AI in diagnostics and patient care, less is known about its effectiveness in patient education, especially in the context of specific medical procedures like colonoscopy [ ]. The primary aim of this study is to assess the degree of concordance between ChatGPT-4.0 responses and clinical guidelines for pre-colonoscopy patient education. Materials and methods Study design This study utilized a descriptive, guideline-concordance-based design to evaluate the reliability of OpenAI’s ChatGPT-4.0 by comparing its responses to established clinical guidelines for pre-colonoscopy patient guidance. The aim was to determine how well the AI's responses aligned with established clinical guidelines, thus assessing its utility as a potential source of medical advice. Development of patient-like queries To evaluate ChatGPT’s reliability in pre-colonoscopy education, 25 simulated patient queries were developed to reflect common concerns encountered in clinical practice. These covered five key domains essential to colonoscopy preparation: dietary recommendations, bowel preparation protocols, cardiovascular medication management (including anticoagulants and antiplatelets), antibiotic prophylaxis, and diabetes medication adjustments. The queries were designed by the first author based on frequently asked patient questions and were reviewed for clinical accuracy and relevance by the senior author, a gastroenterologist with over a decade of experience. The selection of 25 queries was deemed sufficient to ensure a representative sampling across the most relevant and guideline-covered aspects of pre-procedural care. Interaction with ChatGPT Each query was presented to ChatGPT 4.0 in a separate session, mimicking distinct patient interactions. The queries were entered between May 22, 2023, and May 30, 2023. This approach was designed to prevent any learning or bias from previous queries, and it ensured that the AI’s response was independent and uninfluenced by prior questions. Guideline selection for comparative analysis We utilized guidelines from prominent medical societies such as the European Society of Gastrointestinal Endoscopy (ESGE), the U.S. Multi-Society Task Force on Colorectal Cancer (USMSTF), the American College of Gastroenterology-Canadian Association of Gastroenterology (ACG-CAG), the American College of Cardiology-American Heart Association (ACC-AHA), the American Society for Gastrointestinal Endoscopy (ASGE), and the Australian Diabetes Society (ADS) for comparison. These guidelines are considered benchmarks in their respective areas and offer a comprehensive standard against which the AI's responses were evaluated. Analysis of ChatGPT responses Two authors independently evaluated the responses generated by ChatGPT-4.0 and categorized them based on their concordance with established clinical guidelines. Responses were classified into three categories: completely aligned, partially aligned, or not aligned. A response was considered completely aligned if it was fully consistent with the guideline's recommendations, without any omissions or inaccuracies. Partially aligned responses included those that reflected some aspects of the guideline but lacked complete detail or omitted key components. Not aligned responses were those that contradicted or failed to reflect the relevant guideline recommendations. This structured classification approach was implemented to ensure a standardized and unbiased assessment of the AI’s accuracy. Any discrepancies between the two reviewers were resolved through discussion and consensus. Ethical considerations Given the use of a publicly accessible AI and the absence of patient-specific data, the study did not require Institutional Review Board (IRB) approval. This aligns with ethical standards for research involving public data sources where no human subjects are directly involved. Data management and analysis The responses were systematically logged in Microsoft Excel (Microsoft® Corp., Redmond, WA, USA), which facilitated an organized comparison with the guidelines. For each query-response pair, the corresponding guideline was referenced. Results All 25 responses from ChatGPT-4.0 were categorized as completely aligned with the corresponding established clinical guidelines (Table ). This unanimous alignment was observed across a diverse range of pre-colonoscopy care topics, affirming the accuracy and reliability of AI-generated medical advice. ChatGPT's advice adhered strictly to the ESGE and USMSTF guidelines on diet before colonoscopy, emphasizing the necessity of a low-fiber diet and the avoidance of solid foods the day before the procedure. This unanimous alignment was observed across a diverse range of pre-colonoscopy care topics, affirming the accuracy and reliability of AI-generated medical advice. ChatGPT's advice adhered strictly to the ESGE and USMSTF guidelines on diet before colonoscopy, emphasizing the necessity of a low-fiber diet and the avoidance of solid foods the day before the procedure. Questions related to the use of medications like Gas-X and instructions for bowel cleansing agents were accurately addressed by ChatGPT. The AI's responses provided clear, detailed instructions on the preparation process, including the timing and method of bowel cleansing agents according to the ESGE and USMSTF guidelines. ChatGPT's guidance was fully aligned with ACC-AHA and ASGE guidelines on management of antiplatelets and anticoagulants prior to colonoscopy. Furthermore, ChatGPT adeptly handled queries regarding antibiotic prophylaxis for patients with various medical devices or conditions, such as prosthetic heart valves and heart valve infections. The responses were in complete concordance with the ASGE guidelines. ChatGPT's responses to questions about insulin and oral diabetes medication prior to colonoscopy were consistent with guidelines from the ADS. Discussion The growing demand for gastrointestinal procedures, especially among older adults and patients taking complex medications like anticoagulants, creates significant challenges in both pre-procedure preparation and patient education. These challenges generate numerous inquiries from both patients and primary care physicians, underscoring the need for accessible, accurate, and standardized medical guidance [ - ]. In this context, AI-driven tools, particularly large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT, have emerged as a potential solution to bridge gaps in patient education and enhance healthcare efficiency [ , , ]. While ChatGPT has been one of the most widely studied LLMs in the medical field, other advanced models such as Google’s Gemini (formerly Bard), Anthropic’s Claude, DeepSeek, Meta’s LLaMA, and Perplexity AI are rapidly evolving and demonstrating capabilities in generating medically relevant information. Our study systematically evaluated the reliability of OpenAI’s ChatGPT-4.0 in providing pre-colonoscopy guidance and found a high degree of concordance between AI-generated responses and established clinical guidelines. ChatGPT-4.0 delivered accurate recommendations across key domains, including dietary restrictions, bowel preparation, anticoagulation management, and medication use, reinforcing its potential role in clinical practice [ , ]. These findings align with the growing body of research suggesting that AI-driven models can enhance medical education, patient compliance, and procedural outcomes when effectively integrated into clinical workflows [ , ]. LLMs such as ChatGPT have demonstrated promise in patient education by offering structured, guideline-adherent recommendations. The ability of ChatGPT-4.0 to generate responses that are both medically accurate and comprehensible to patients highlights its potential as a valuable adjunct for gastroenterologists and primary care physicians in improving pre-colonoscopy preparation. Previous studies indicate that gastroenterologists overwhelmingly recognize ChatGPT’s reliability, with 80% agreeing that it provides accurate information, 90% believing it can reduce medication errors, and 100% acknowledging its potential in streamlining patient education [ - ]. Despite these strengths, LLMs also present inherent challenges. A primary concern is the phenomenon of AI “hallucination,” wherein models may generate factually incorrect, exaggerated, or misleading information. In some cases, responses may include over-explaining, unnecessary hyperbole, or confidently presented inaccuracies, particularly when prompts are vague or ambiguous. These issues arise from the probabilistic nature of language generation and limitations in training methodologies. While refining training datasets and implementing real-world clinical validation are critical strategies to mitigate these risks, another essential factor is prompt design. Research has shown that well-structured, specific, and contextually framed prompts can significantly improve the accuracy and relevance of AI-generated responses. Therefore, clinicians and researchers using LLMs must be equipped with a basic understanding of effective prompt engineering to maximize the utility of these tools while minimizing misinformation. Although our study did not observe significant hallucinations in ChatGPT-4.0’s responses, responsible use requires ongoing vigilance and user education as AI technologies continue to evolve [ , ]. Several additional limitations warrant consideration. First, our study employed a structured set of queries, which may not fully capture the diverse and nuanced ways in which real patients phrase their questions. Second, while ChatGPT-4.0 demonstrated high accuracy, it does not provide individualized medical advice, as it lacks access to patient-specific factors such as comorbidities, previous procedures, and personal health history. These constraints highlight the need for AI applications to complement, rather than replace, clinician-patient interactions. Another critical concern is data privacy and regulatory compliance. Prior studies report that only 10% of gastroenterologists express confidence in ChatGPT’s ability to uphold patient confidentiality and comply with privacy regulations, underscoring significant security concerns [ ]. These concerns align with broader debates on AI implementation in healthcare, emphasizing the necessity for stringent oversight to ensure adherence to regulatory standards such as the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA). Another critical concern is data privacy and regulatory compliance. Prior studies report that only 10% of gastroenterologists express confidence in ChatGPT’s ability to uphold patient confidentiality and comply with privacy regulations, underscoring significant security concerns [ ]. These concerns align with broader debates on AI implementation in healthcare, emphasizing the necessity for stringent oversight to ensure adherence to regulatory standards such as the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA). While AI holds considerable potential to enhance patient education and workflow efficiency, its role should be that of a complementary tool rather than a replacement for human clinicians. Many physicians have voiced concerns that over-reliance on AI could erode the physician-patient relationship, reinforcing the importance of maintaining human oversight in patient interactions [ ]. AI models should be deployed to augment clinician decision-making rather than supplant it, ensuring that patient care remains grounded in empathy, critical thinking, and professional expertise. Our study did not compare ChatGPT-4.0 with other AI tools, such as DeepSeek, Gemini/Bard, Claude, or LLaMA, which have demonstrated advancements in AI-driven medical applications. While previous research suggests that ChatGPT-4.0 outperforms both its predecessor (ChatGPT-3.5) and Google’s Bard in accuracy and coherence [ , ], the rapid evolution of AI necessitates continuous reassessment of these models’ effectiveness and safety in clinical settings. Moving forward, the integration of AI into gastroenterology should prioritize improvements in data privacy, response accuracy, and the long-term impact of AI-assisted patient education on clinical outcomes. Future research should evaluate AI’s efficacy in real-world patient interactions, particularly its ability to dynamically respond to diverse patient concerns. Additionally, further studies are needed to validate AI-driven guidance across varied patient populations and healthcare settings. Furthermore, the absence of patient-specific context in ChatGPT’s responses presents a significant limitation in clinical workflows. Real-world decision-making often requires consideration of factors such as comorbid conditions, medication interactions, prior procedural outcomes, and social determinants of health details that AI models currently cannot assess. As a result, when discrepancies arise between AI-generated suggestions and individualized clinical judgment, physicians should prioritize tailored decision-making. Clinicians are advised to interpret AI outputs as preliminary guidance that must be contextualized within the broader clinical picture. Establishing clear protocols for reviewing AI recommendations, incorporating human oversight, and fostering patient communication will be essential to safely integrating such tools into routine care. As AI continues to reshape medical practice, its implementation should be guided by the principles of accuracy, security, and patient-centered care. Ongoing evaluation and refinement will be essential to ensuring that AI technologies enhance, rather than undermine, clinical decision-making and physician-patient relationships. Conclusions This study shows that ChatGPT-4.0 provides pre-colonoscopy guidance fully aligned with established clinical guidelines from multiple medical societies. This consistency highlights its potential as a reliable tool for standardized patient education, improving information dissemination, and reducing the workload of healthcare providers.
